name: Battle of Adrianople
info: Gothic rebels under Fritigern defeated the Eastern Roman army and killed the emperor Valens near Adrianople in Thrace in 378, during the Gothic War of 376 to 382.

facts.place: Within a few hours' march of Adrianople (modern Edirne, European Turkey), in the Roman province of Thracia; the exact site is disputed, with three locations proposed north and east of the city
facts.sides: The Eastern Roman army under the emperor Valens, perhaps as many as 15,000 men by some modern estimates, and Gothic rebels led by Fritigern, joined by the cavalry of Alatheus and Saphrax and by Alans, put by several modern historians at 12,000 to 15,000
facts.outcome: The Roman army was routed and Valens died, though how is uncertain; the Goths then failed to take Adrianople.

t: Valens marched out against the advice of some of his officers and without waiting for the western emperor Gratian, whose reinforcements were on their way, and he rejected Fritigern's offer of peace and an alliance the day before.
The Gothic cavalry came back from foraging after the fighting had begun, and surrounded Roman troops who were already in disarray; Fritigern's talks had gained the time needed for its return.
Historians disagree about the battle's weight: Charles Oman saw heavy cavalry replacing Roman infantry, while T. S. Burns called it mainly a fight of infantry against infantry.
dyk: Valens's body was never found, and two stories of his death circulated: that he died anonymously on the field, or that he was burned in a peasant's cottage after the Goths set it on fire.
ev: Goths led by Alavivus and Fritigern are admitted across the Danube as allies and revolt after hardships under the commanders Lupicinus and Maximus
Romans and Goths fight the Battle of the Willows, which ends as a bloody draw
Valens reaches Constantinople on 30 May and sends Sebastianus to reorganise the armies in Thrace
On 8 August Fritigern offers peace and an alliance in exchange for Roman territory, and Valens refuses
On 9 August the Romans march out from Adrianople and are routed by the Goths and their cavalry, and Valens dies
The Goths try and fail to take Adrianople
Theodosius I is made emperor on 19 January
Peace is declared on 3 October and the Goths settle inside the Empire as foederati

sections.background:
In 376 the Goths, led by Alavivus and Fritigern, asked to be allowed to settle in the Eastern Roman Empire after the Huns had displaced them. The emperor Valens, hoping they would become farmers and soldiers, admitted them as allies (foederati). Once across the Danube, the dishonesty of the Roman provincial commanders Lupicinus and Maximus led the newcomers to revolt after many hardships. Officials under Lupicinus sold off much of the food meant for the Goths, and Gothic families sold children into slavery for dog meat. At Marcianople Lupicinus ordered Fritigern and Alavivus held hostage and their retainers killed, then released Fritigern, and the Goths rebelled.

Valens asked the western emperor Gratian for reinforcements, and Gratian sent the general Frigeridus and the leader of his guards, Richomeres. For the next two years there was a series of running battles with no clear victories for either side, among them the Battle of the Willows in 377, a bloody draw in which the Roman left wing began to collapse before it was reinforced. Valens had meanwhile been kept in the East by negotiations with Persia and a Saracen uprising.

In 378 Valens decided to take control himself and assembled troops from his own resources in Syria and from the reserves of the Western Roman Empire in Gaul. He reached Constantinople on 30 May and appointed Sebastianus, newly arrived from Italy, to reorganise the armies in Thrace. Gratian's army, meanwhile, was delayed when the Lentienses, part of the Alamanni, attacked across the Rhine.
sections.forces:
Valens's army may have drawn on three field armies: the Army of Thrace, which may have lost heavily in 376 and 377, and the 1st and 2nd Armies in the Emperor's Presence, which had been committed to the Persian frontier in 376 and sent west in 377 and 378. It included veterans and consisted of seven legions of 700 to 1,000 men each, with a cavalry of mounted archers and the imperial guard, the Scholae. Some modern historians put the Roman strength at as many as 15,000 men, 10,000 infantry and 5,000 cavalry. Another estimate puts the original force at 40,000. Warren Treadgold's figures for the three armies are for 395 and include units formed after Adrianople, and not all three armies are likely to have fought together.

The Goths were probably in two armies south of the Danube. Fritigern led one, recruited largely from the Therving exiles, and Alatheus and Saphrax led another, recruited largely from the Greuthung exiles, whose cavalry took part with Alans. The Gothic armies were mostly infantry, with some cavalry. Roman scouts counted 10,000 Goths, a figure Ammianus Marcellinus dismissed as too low, since Alatheus and Saphrax's men were away. Several modern historians put the Gothic strength at 12,000 to 15,000, and more recent scholarship mostly holds that the two armies were similar in size.

Valens fortified his camp at Adrianople with ditches and ramparts. He learned on 6 August that about 10,000 Goths were advancing from a position 25 kilometres to the north. Part of the Gothic cavalry was out foraging at a distance, and Valens's estimate of the numbers left it out.
sections.course:
On 8 August Fritigern sent an emissary proposing peace and an alliance in exchange for Roman territory. Valens, sure of victory because of his supposed numerical superiority, rejected it. Richomeres had brought a letter from Gratian asking Valens to wait for reinforcements, and Valens's officers also advised waiting, but Valens decided to fight. On the morning of 9 August he left the imperial treasury and administration under guard in Adrianople and marched north, arriving around noon after eight miles over difficult terrain.

The Romans came tired and dehydrated to the Gothic camp on a hilltop. The Goths, except for their cavalry, held a circle of wagons that held their families and possessions. Fritigern wished to delay the Romans until the cavalry came back. The Goths burned the fields so that smoke harassed the Romans, and negotiations for an exchange of hostages began, which exasperated the Roman soldiers but gained Fritigern time.

Some Roman units began the battle without orders, believing victory would be easy. The imperial scholae of shield-archers under the Iberian prince Bacurius attacked and, lacking support, were pushed back. The Roman left wing then reached the wagon circle, but too late: the Gothic cavalry returned from foraging and surrounded the Romans, who were already in disarray. They fell back to the foot of the hill, unable to manoeuvre in their heavy armour and with long shields, and casualties, exhaustion and pressure turned into a rout. The killing went on until nightfall.

The emperor was abandoned by his guards; most of the cavalry fled.
sections.aftermath:
According to Ammianus, the Goths marched at once to Adrianople and tried to take it, and failed. Many Roman soldiers who had not been let into the city fought the besiegers below the walls. A third of the Roman army retreated, and the losses were beyond counting. By another account two thirds of the army lay dead, and the total loss may have been as high as 26,000 of an original 40,000. Many officers fell, among them Sebastianus, Traianus, the tribune Aequitius and thirty-five senior officers, while Ricomer, Victor and Saturninus escaped.

The Goths, together with some Huns and Alans, went on to Perinthus and Constantinople, where they were fended off, and then plundered the countryside again. Valens had died without a successor in the East. The magister militum Julius had the Goths near the frontier lured together and killed, and when word of this reached the Goths in the interior provinces in 379, some rioted, especially in Asia Minor, and the Romans put down the riots and killed Goths there too.

Theodosius was made emperor on 19 January 379, and the sources say little of how. Peace was declared on 3 October 382. The Goths recognised the emperor's authority and served as foederati, but unlike earlier practice they were given land in Scythia, Moesia and possibly Macedonia, under their own authority and not dispersed. Fritigern, Alatheus and Saphrax are not mentioned again in the ancient histories.
sections.sources:
The main source is Ammianus Marcellinus, whose detailed contemporary account of the lead-up to the battle, from the Roman side, forms the end of his history. He names the officers in Valens's army and a few of its units. A list of the army's units survives in the eastern Notitia Dignitatum, which dates from after Theodosius, so an order of battle cannot be drawn up: many units it names were formed after Adrianople or moved there later.

Where the sources differ, Ammianus has Sebastianus urging an immediate attack and Victor advising a wait for Gratian, while Eunapius has Sebastianus saying they should wait. The sources are few for the years 379 to 382. Of Valens's end nothing certain is known: the story that he was burned in a cottage circulated after the battle.

Historians dispute the site, which lay within a few hours' march of the city. One thesis puts it north of the city between the Tonzos and Hebros rivers, another east of the Tonzos near Muratçalı, and a third east of the city near Demirhanlı. The numbers on both sides are estimates. Older works held that overwhelming Gothic numbers, Gothic cavalry and the stirrup explain the Gothic victory; more recent works mostly hold that the armies were of similar size, that the infantry mattered more than the cavalry, and that neither side used stirrups until the 6th century.
sections.legacy:
As part of the Gothic War of 376 to 382, the battle is often considered the start of the events which led to the fall of the Western Roman Empire in the 5th century, although the war's significance is widely debated. It was the worst Roman defeat since the Battle of Edessa. It destroyed the core of the East Roman army and killed valuable administrators, and the lack of reserves worsened a recruitment crisis. It did not end the Empire, since imperial military power was only temporarily crippled.

The Goths, though partly tamed by Theodosius I, who accepted them once more as allied tribes, were never expelled, exterminated or assimilated. They remained a distinct entity within the frontiers, for a few years allies, later semi-independent or fully independent, and often hostile. The Therving Goths could now negotiate with Rome as a unified people inside the borders, and would become the Visigoths. This change in Rome's relationship with the barbarians would lead to the sack of Rome in 410.

Valens had been an Arian Christian, and his death helped pave the way for Theodosius to make Nicene Christianity the Empire's official form; the Goths, like many peoples beyond the frontier, converted to Arianism. For the art of war, Charles Oman wrote in 1885 that the battle was a turning point, with heavy cavalry triumphing over Roman infantry and ushering in the age of the medieval knight. T. S. Burns disputed this in 1973, writing that the Gothic cavalry was fairly small, that Valens would have had more cavalry, and that the battle was mainly infantry against infantry.

summary: On 9 August 378 near Adrianople, Gothic rebels under Fritigern, joined by cavalry that came back from foraging, routed the Eastern Roman army and the emperor Valens died. The Goths failed to take the city, and peace in 382 let them settle inside the Empire as allies.
notes: Roman strength: first article gives 'as many as 15,000' (some modern historians); second gives 40,000 original force and 26,000 lost. Both given.
Casualties: first article says a third retreated, losses uncountable; second says two thirds dead. Both given. The first article's 'destroyed nearly all armories' and 'crushing blow' left out.

Roman left wing: first article says it reached the wagon circle before the Gothic cavalry arrived; second says it was surrounded and destroyed after the cavalry arrived. Both are compatible in my text, but the editor should read it.
Who began the battle without orders: first article names the scholae shield-archers under Bacurius; second names Scutarii under Cassio and Sagittarii under Bacurius.
Time of arrival: first article says around noon, second says around two in the afternoon; only noon given.
Battle of Argentaria (first article) is called Argentovaria in the second; not named in text.
Valens's death: two stories in first article (on the field anonymously; burned in a cottage); second has a farmhouse story and a slain-in-combat story. Body never found.

Left out: Ammianus's passages on atrocities, the Arab with the loincloth at Constantinople, Themistius's long quotations, details of the Notitia and each named officer's role, Gothic leaders' fate speculation.

The article's sentence that Traianus was 'supposedly still alive when Valens sought refuge with the Lanciarii and Mattiarii' conflicts with the second article's list of the slain; I listed Traianus among the dead on the second article's authority.
